## Glossary {#glossary}

The four terms below, which follow the definitions given by @NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms, are not interchangeable, and the course depends on the distinction between these terms, since a finding can survive every robustness check on its own data and still fail on new data, or survive the checks and still be one that nobody can recompute from the original materials.

| Term | Definition | In this course |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Reproducibility** | Same question, same data, same analysis → same result | Tested across the SCORE sample by @MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial. In the Europeanisation case study, the result reported by the original author (OA) was not reproducible from the original materials, and the class reproduces in Task 3 a value recorded for one of the analysts in the robustness study of SCORE [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] |
| **Robustness** | Same question, same data, justifiable alternative analysis → stable result | The design of the robustness study; the five analysts of the claim; the specification menu and the curve of the claim in Tasks 4 and 5, with 864 specifications |
| **Replicability** | Same question, independent new data → same result | Tested across the SCORE sample by @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial. For the claim of the Europeanisation case study, a replication on later Eurobarometer waves was judged not successful |
| **Repeatability** | Umbrella term covering all three above | Used in the glossary of Nosek and colleagues as the overarching category |

### The SCORE dossier {#the-europeanisation-case-score-dossier-one-paper-all-three-rs}

The target article [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic] went through all three SCORE activities, which reached three different verdicts on the same paper: the reproduction failed twice, in different ways, the reanalysis by the five analysts of the robustness study agreed in sign while its recorded effect sizes ranged from −0.006 to −0.452, and the preregistered replication on later Eurobarometer waves was judged not successful (first report b = +0.002, p = .046, N = 352,114; report revised in October 2026 b = +0.001, SE 0.0007, t = 1.428, p = 0.153, N = 331,668). The parent node of the dossier is <https://osf.io/h7432/>, whose components are described node by node in the [repositories module](companion/repositories.qmd#sec-trail-europeanisation), while the [background page](background.qmd#sec-repetition) presents the case in full.

## Core readings

### The three *Nature* 2026 papers (SCORE)

- **Reproducibility:** @MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial – how often the central result of a paper can be recomputed from its own data. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10203-5>
- **Robustness:** @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness – the robustness study (Multi100), in which at least five analysts reanalysed each of a hundred claims. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09844-9>
- **Replicability:** @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial – how often claims hold on new data, under preregistered protocols. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-10078-y>
- @AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen – the SCORE programme, of which all three studies are part. <https://doi.org/10.31235/osf.io/46mnb>

### Vocabulary

- @NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms – a four-page glossary of the terms of repeatability; read it before the day. <https://doi.org/10.31222/osf.io/mqfp4_v1>
- @NosekErrington2020WhatReplication – what counts as a replication. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000691>

### Estimands and analytical choices

- @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand – the steps from a theoretical estimand to an empirical one, and why a result means little until the estimand is stated. <https://doi.org/10.1177/00031224211004187>
- @SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne – the red-card study, in which twenty-nine teams analysed one dataset. <https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245917747646>
- @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial – the reanalysis of the red-card study that traced the spread of its results to teams answering different questions. <https://doi.org/10.1177/23780231211024421>

### The multiverse and its critics

- @SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology and @GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience – how undisclosed flexibility in analysis produces false positives, and the garden of forking paths.
- @SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse and @SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis – the multiverse analysis and the specification curve, the two proposals on which the curve of the claim draws.
- @DelGiudiceGangestad2021TravelersGuideMultiverse – a systematic framework for judging which analytic decisions are equivalent, and so which analyses belong in one multiverse.
- @BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers – a many-analysts study in which teams tested one hypothesis about immigration and social policy on the same data.
- @Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed – the case for a few thoughtful models over billions of regressions.
- @RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood and @LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne – what a multiverse is good for, and the argument that a fully specified question has only one correct analysis.
- @HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom – the multiverse as a teaching device.
- [Inference on the curve](curve.qmd#inference) – in the day format, the course reading for the final part: why a large set of results is not a large set of independent tests, and what a single test across the whole curve can and cannot establish.

The readings listed above are examined against the curve of the claim in the [companion module on the multiverse](companion/multiverse.qmd).

### Preregistration

None of the three readings below is required, since everything is taught in the course, but the readings allow you to arrive with the ideas already in hand, and all three are open access.

- Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven & Mellor (2018). The preregistration revolution. *PNAS*, 115(11), 2600–2606. <https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1708274114> – a short primer on the idea on which preregistration depends: predicting a result against explaining one after the fact, and the case, like ours, where the data already exist.
- The AsPredicted eight-question form – the short template on which the preregistration block of your report is modelled, listed on the OSF as the "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org". Live form: <https://aspredicted.org>; OSF listing: <https://help.osf.io/article/158-create-a-preregistration>.
- van den Akker, Weston, Campbell, et al. (2021). Preregistration of secondary data analysis: A template and tutorial. *Meta-Psychology*, 5, 2625. <https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2020.2625> – the fuller template, built for our situation of reanalysing data that already exist, and the tool that a full version of the exercise would use.

## Companion

The modules of the [companion](companion/index.qmd), each written on the data of this case study, contain the teaching that a single day can only mention, and the companion index lists every module with a line describing it. The guidance on installing R and an IDE, the setup help and the modules on the tools, from [Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html) to [Quarto documents](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/quarto.html) and [Git and GitHub](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/git-github.html), are provided on the [AR4DS site](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/).

## If you are at Newcastle University
